idiom_name: JVM JOSE libraries from Kotlin (Nimbus JOSE+JWT, JJWT, Auth0 java-jwt); Ktor supplies the verifying side
implementation_notes: Kotlin has no JOSE support in its standard library, so the builder is a JVM library driven from Kotlin: Nimbus (JWTClaimsSet.Builder, JWSHeader.Builder, RSASSASigner, SignedJWT) or JJWT's fluent Jwts.builder() produce the compact assertion, and the Kotlin-flavoured part is a data class for the claim set plus a typed key id. What replaces the classic structure: the library's builder and signer replace the AssertionBuilder class, and the code that remains is typically one object with a sign(principal, audience): String function that owns issuer, TTL and the mandatory claims; Ktor's ktor-server-auth-jwt installs only the consumer side (Bearer verification plus payload validation), which is why issuance still belongs to the library call. Coroutines change nothing here - signing is CPU-bound and short, so a suspend wrapper is optional, not a design requirement.
code_sketch:
val issuedAt = Date()
val claims = JWTClaimsSet.Builder()
    .subject(userId)
    .issuer("https://idp.example")
    .audience("https://api.example")
    .issueTime(issuedAt)
    .expirationTime(Date(issuedAt.time + 300_000))
    .jwtID(randomUUID().toString())
    .build()
val jwt = SignedJWT(
    JWSHeader.Builder(JWSAlgorithm.RS256).keyID(kid).build(), claims)
jwt.sign(RSASSASigner(privateRsaJwk))
val assertion: String = jwt.serialize()
pitfalls: Constructing RSASSASigner per call re-parses the JWK; keep one signer per key in a val (and remember it is not a coroutine-safe substitute for a proper key store).
Mixing JOSE libraries on one classpath (Nimbus plus JJWT) works until their providers or shadowed classes collide, surfacing as runtime configuration errors rather than compile errors.
Kotlin's default arguments make it easy to write a helper whose exp defaults to null; a null time claim must fail issuance rather than quietly mint a non-expiring assertion.
